questions.q: Why isn't quoting symmetrically around fair value enough once a market maker holds inventory?
options: Symmetric quotes around fair value give no particular reason to attract trades that reduce inventory -- the maker is equally likely to get more long as to get flatter, leaving unwanted risk unaddressed
Fair value becomes mathematically undefined once inventory is non-zero
Regulations require quotes to shift away from fair value when inventory is held
Symmetric quoting around fair value is always more profitable regardless of inventory
questions.explain: Holding inventory creates directional risk; quoting symmetrically around fair value does nothing to actively encourage returning to flat, leaving that risk unaddressed.

questions.q: In the reservation price formula r = s - gamma*q*sigma^2*(T-t), what happens to r when inventory q is positive (long)?
options: r sits below fair value s, shifting both quotes down to make the ask more competitive and encourage selling
r sits above fair value s, making the bid more competitive
r equals fair value exactly regardless of q
r becomes undefined when q is positive
questions.explain: A positive q makes the whole subtracted term positive, pulling r below s -- shifting both quotes down, which makes the ask easier to hit (encouraging a sale) and the bid harder to hit.

questions.q: In the worked example (fair value 100.00, inventory +500, reservation price 99.775), why do BOTH the bid and the ask end up below fair value, not just one of them?
options: The entire quoting center (the reservation price) shifted down due to inventory, and both bid and ask are placed symmetrically around that shifted center
Only the ask shifts down; the bid always stays at fair value regardless of inventory
This is a calculation error -- only one quote should move
Bid and ask always move in opposite directions from each other, never the same direction
questions.explain: Since bid and ask are placed symmetrically around the reservation price (not around fair value directly), shifting the reservation price shifts both quotes together in the same direction.

questions.q: Why does this lesson leave the exact spread-width formula to a later lesson, treating it as a given parameter here?
options: To isolate the reservation-price mechanism, which has well-agreed-upon behavior, separate from spread-width constants that are genuinely debated and tuned empirically in real implementations
Because spread width has nothing to do with market making
Because the reservation price formula already determines the spread width automatically
Because calculating spread width requires information not yet covered anywhere in this course
questions.explain: The lesson deliberately separates two different concerns: the reservation price shift (well-established) and spread sizing (genuinely debated and empirically calibrated in practice).

questions.q: A market maker is short 300 shares (q = -300). What happens to its reservation price and quote competitiveness?
options: The reservation price shifts above fair value, making the bid more competitive than the ask, encouraging a buy back toward flat
The reservation price shifts below fair value, making the ask more competitive
The reservation price stays exactly at fair value since -300 is treated the same as 0
The reservation price becomes undefined for negative inventory
questions.explain: Negative q flips the sign of the inventory term, pushing r above fair value -- shifting both quotes up, which makes the bid more attractive to hit, encouraging a buy back to flat.
